That assumption is contradicted by the fictional curator’s request for 35–50 word display labels after approving a 42-word draft [sequence 6], and by the report that a 190-word label went unread because it did not fit [sequence 7]. Routine visitors read the first sentence and large-print species name but usually skipped the provenance appendix [sequence 5], suggesting that visible, concise content may improve exposure; this observation does not prove comprehension or imply that provenance is unimportant. The short-label failure was attributed to an unsupported wild-pollinator claim [sequence 7]; specimen observations establish only that three of twelve buds opened in an indoor trial and flowers opened after sunset and closed the next morning [sequence 4]. These are reported observations, not evidence about wild pollinators. Trial A is an approval report, not a guarantee for future labels. A useful revision should guide the writer toward concise, observed details and off-label supporting information, while retaining uncertainty and avoiding claims of general acceptance."
